question: How do I hire a fractional CRO in Scottsdale?
body:
## Direct Answer

To hire a fractional CRO in Scottsdale, define the revenue outcome you need first (pipeline, retention, or a fundraise-readiness sales engine), then source part-time chief revenue officers through Arizona operator networks, fractional-executive marketplaces, and warm referrals from local SaaS founders. Expect to pay roughly $200 to $400 per hour or a $8,000 to $20,000 monthly retainer for one to three days a week, and scope the engagement to a 90-day proof-of-value before committing to a longer term.

A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is a senior go-to-market leader who owns your full revenue function — sales, marketing alignment, RevOps, and customer success handoffs — on a part-time, fixed-scope basis instead of a full-time salaried seat. For Scottsdale companies, the calculus is especially attractive: the metro has a dense cluster of B2B SaaS, med-tech, fintech, and professional-services firms that have outgrown a founder-led sales motion but cannot yet justify a $300K-plus base plus equity for a full-time CRO. This essay walks through how to scope the role, where to actually find qualified operators locally, what to pay, how to vet them, and how to structure the first 90 days so the hire pays for itself.

## What does a fractional CRO actually do for a Scottsdale company?

The core job of a fractional CRO is to install a repeatable, measurable revenue system where one does not yet exist. In practice that means auditing your current funnel end to end, diagnosing where deals stall, rebuilding your sales process and forecasting discipline, and putting the right metrics, comp plans, and tooling in place so growth stops depending on the founder's personal Rolodex. A good fractional CRO is a builder and an operator, not just an advisor who drops a deck and disappears — they roll up their sleeves inside your CRM, sit in on real deal reviews, and coach your existing reps.

For a Scottsdale business specifically, the fractional model maps well onto the local growth stage. Many companies here are in the $2M to $30M revenue band — past product-market fit, generating real pipeline, but still running sales on instinct. That is exactly the window where a seasoned revenue leader delivers outsized return, because the fixes are structural (process, segmentation, forecasting, comp) rather than heroic. The fractional arrangement lets a company that could never recruit a Fortune 500 CRO borrow that caliber of thinking for one to three days a week. It is worth being clear-eyed about the boundary, though: a fractional CRO leads and architects, but they are not a full-time individual contributor who will personally close your entire quarter. If what you actually need is a bag-carrying salesperson, that is a different hire. For a fuller breakdown of where the role begins and ends, see the PULSE library entry on [the fractional CRO scope of work](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-scope).

The best engagements start with a diagnosis, not a mandate. A strong operator will spend their first weeks listening — to reps, to churned customers, to the founder — before they touch the comp plan. Treat any candidate who arrives with a fixed playbook and no curiosity about your specific motion as a red flag.

## How do I find qualified fractional CRO candidates in Scottsdale?

There is no single storefront for fractional revenue leaders, so the most reliable approach is to run several sourcing channels in parallel and let referrals do the heavy lifting on trust. Scottsdale and the wider Phoenix metro have a genuinely deep bench of go-to-market talent — a lot of it seeded by companies like GoDaddy, Infusionsoft/Keap, Axon, and a growing wave of venture-backed SaaS — and much of that talent has moved into portfolio and fractional work rather than another full-time seat.

Start with the warm channels, because they carry the most signal. Ask your investors, your fractional CFO, your board members, and two or three founder peers who they have personally seen build revenue. Local operator communities are the second layer: the Arizona Technology Council, StartupAZ, PHX Startup Week, and the various RevGenius and Pavilion chapters that meet in the Valley are full of leaders who consult on the side. Beyond warm intros, the fractional-executive marketplaces — Chief Outsiders, Continuum, GrowthForce-style GTM firms, Bolster, and Go Fractional — let you filter by function and stage, and several maintain Southwest-region rosters.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Define revenue problem] --> B[Warm referrals from investors and founders]
  A --> C[Arizona operator networks]
  A --> D[Fractional executive marketplaces]
  B --> E[Shortlist of three to five candidates]
  C --> E
  D --> E
  E --> F[Structured vetting and reference checks]
  F --> G[Ninety day paid pilot]
  G --> H[Extend or exit decision]
```

When you evaluate the source, weigh proximity honestly. A fractional CRO does not have to live in Scottsdale — most of this work is done over video, in your CRM, and in weekly deal reviews — but a leader who can be in the room for a quarterly kickoff, a key customer, or a tough comp conversation adds value that Zoom cannot fully replace. If you want local presence, say so up front and prioritize candidates in the Phoenix metro or those who commit to a set number of on-site days per quarter. For a deeper comparison of remote versus in-market fractional leaders, the PULSE guide on [sourcing part-time revenue executives](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/sourcing-fractional-execs) breaks down the trade-offs by company stage.

## What should I pay a fractional CRO in the Scottsdale market?

Fractional CRO pricing generally follows one of three structures, and understanding all three keeps you from overpaying or, worse, underpaying for a leader who then disengages. The most common is a monthly retainer tied to a committed number of days per week. In most U.S. markets, including Scottsdale, that lands somewhere between roughly $8,000 and $20,000 per month for one to three days of weekly involvement, with the range driven by the operator's pedigree, the complexity of your revenue motion, and how hands-on the engagement is. Hourly arrangements exist for lighter advisory work and typically run $200 to $400 per hour. A third structure blends a smaller base retainer with performance upside tied to pipeline or revenue milestones — attractive on paper, but only worth it when the metrics are clean and both sides trust the attribution.

Anchor these numbers against the alternative. A full-time CRO in a market like Scottsdale commands a base commonly in the $250K to $350K range, plus variable comp and equity, which puts the fully loaded cost well past $400K a year before you have proven the person fits. A fractional retainer at $15K a month is $180K annualized at the top of a heavy engagement, and most companies run lighter than that. The point of the model is not simply to spend less — it is to buy senior judgment at a stage where a full-time seat would be both unaffordable and underutilized.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Engagement model] --> B[Monthly retainer]
  A --> C[Hourly advisory]
  A --> D[Base plus performance]
  B --> E[Eight thousand to twenty thousand per month]
  C --> F[Two hundred to four hundred per hour]
  D --> G[Lower base plus milestone bonus]
  E --> H[Best for hands on rebuilds]
  F --> I[Best for light advisory]
  G --> J[Best when metrics are clean]
```

Beware of the two failure modes at the price extremes. Pay too little and you get an advisor stretched across a dozen clients who never truly owns your outcome. Pay a premium retainer but scope the engagement to one day a week, and you have bought a very expensive sounding board. Match the day-count to the actual scope of work: a full revenue-engine rebuild genuinely needs two to three days a week for the first quarter, while ongoing steady-state coaching can taper to one. For a structured way to model the return, the PULSE breakdown on [fractional executive cost versus a full-time hire](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cost-benefit) walks through the loaded-cost math.

## How do I vet a fractional CRO before signing?

Vetting a fractional revenue leader is different from vetting a full-time exec, because you are buying a track record of repeatable outcomes rather than a long-term culture fit. The single most predictive question is not "what did you achieve" but "what did you build, and did it survive after you left." Ask every finalist to walk you through a specific engagement: the state of the revenue function when they arrived, the two or three structural changes they made, the metrics before and after, and — critically — whether the system they installed was still running a year later. Operators who build durable systems will have concrete numbers and will name the things that did not work. Be wary of anyone whose case studies are all unqualified triumphs.

Reference checks matter more here than for almost any other role, and you should insist on speaking with founders they have actually worked with, not curated cheerleaders. Ask those references pointed questions: Did the fractional CRO show up consistently, or drift as they took on new clients? Did they empower the internal team or create dependency on themselves? Would you hire them again, and if not, why? You are looking for signal on reliability and on whether they transfer capability rather than hoard it. It also pays to understand their portfolio load — a fractional leader running six simultaneous clients cannot give any one of them real depth, so ask directly how many engagements they carry and how they protect your day. The PULSE resource on [structuring a fractional executive trial](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-trial-structure) offers a reference-call script and a first-90-days scorecard you can lift directly.

Finally, test for chemistry with your actual team, not just the founder. The fractional CRO will spend most of their time with your reps and your RevOps lead, so put them in a working session — a live deal review or a pipeline audit — before you sign. How they coach in real time tells you more than any interview answer.

## How should I structure the first 90 days?

The first quarter should be scoped as a paid pilot with an explicit exit ramp, because that structure protects both sides and forces clarity about what success looks like. Frame the engagement around a small number of concrete, measurable deliverables rather than a vague mandate to "grow revenue." Typical 90-day outputs include a documented sales process and stage definitions, a rebuilt or validated forecast, a cleaned-up CRM with accurate pipeline hygiene, a revised comp plan aligned to the behaviors you actually want, and a diagnosis of the one or two structural constraints holding growth back. Agree on these deliverables in writing before day one.

Sequence the work so trust compounds. In the first 30 days the operator diagnoses — they interview reps, ride along on calls, audit the funnel, and talk to churned and won customers. Days 30 to 60 are for installing the highest-leverage fixes: process, forecasting cadence, and the metrics that will govern everything after. The final stretch is about handoff and durability — coaching your team to run the system without the fractional leader in every meeting, and setting the agenda for whether the engagement extends, tapers, or ends. Build a clear off-ramp into the contract: a 30-day notice on either side keeps everyone honest and means a poor fit costs you a quarter, not a year. This proof-of-value framing is the throughline that connects everything above — scope, sourcing, price, and vetting all exist to de-risk this first 90 days.

## Related questions

### What is the difference between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant?
A fractional CRO takes ownership of your revenue outcomes and operates inside your team as an interim leader, while a sales consultant advises from the outside and hands you recommendations you must implement yourself.

### Can a fractional CRO work remotely for a Scottsdale company?
Yes — most of the work happens in your CRM and in weekly video deal reviews, but negotiate a set number of on-site days per quarter if in-room presence for kickoffs and key customers matters to you.

### How long does a typical fractional CRO engagement last?
Most run six to eighteen months: an intensive first quarter to rebuild the revenue engine, then a lighter steady-state cadence, tapering as your internal team absorbs the system or as you recruit a full-time leader.

### When should I hire a full-time CRO instead?
Move to full-time when revenue reliably exceeds roughly $20M to $30M, the go-to-market motion is complex enough to demand daily leadership, and you can fully utilize and afford a $400K-plus loaded seat.

### Do fractional CROs work with pre-revenue startups?
Rarely and cautiously — before product-market fit the constraint is usually the product, not the revenue system, so a fractional CRO is most valuable once you have real pipeline to systematize.

## FAQ

**How much does a fractional CRO cost in Scottsdale?**
Expect roughly $8,000 to $20,000 per month for a one-to-three-day-a-week retainer, or $200 to $400 per hour for lighter advisory work. Pricing scales with the operator's pedigree and how hands-on the engagement is.

**What size company benefits most from a fractional CRO?**
Companies in the roughly $2M to $30M revenue band, past product-market fit but not yet able to justify a full-time CRO seat, get the most leverage from the model.

**Where can I find fractional CRO candidates near Scottsdale?**
Warm referrals from investors and founder peers, Arizona operator communities like the Arizona Technology Council and StartupAZ, and fractional-executive marketplaces such as Chief Outsiders, Bolster, and Go Fractional.

**How is a fractional CRO different from a fractional CMO?**
A fractional CRO owns the entire revenue function — sales, forecasting, RevOps, and customer-success alignment — whereas a fractional CMO owns demand generation, brand, and marketing pipeline. In smaller companies the CRO role often absorbs marketing oversight.

**What should be in a fractional CRO contract?**
A defined scope with measurable 90-day deliverables, the committed days per week, the retainer or hourly rate, IP and confidentiality terms, a clear performance-review checkpoint, and a 30-day exit clause on either side.

**How do I measure whether the engagement is working?**
Track leading indicators the CRO can influence quickly — pipeline coverage, forecast accuracy, sales-cycle length, and CRM hygiene — alongside lagging revenue metrics, and review them against the deliverables you agreed to at the start.

**Can a fractional CRO help us raise our next round?**
Yes. A common mandate is to make the revenue engine fundable — clean metrics, a defensible forecast, and a repeatable motion — which is often exactly what investors scrutinize during diligence.

**Should the fractional CRO manage my existing sales team?**
Typically yes. Part of the value is coaching and holding your current reps and RevOps staff accountable to the new system, but confirm reporting lines and authority in the contract so there is no ambiguity for your team.
